questions.question: What is the difference between var and := in Go?
questions.title: var vs := in Go
questions.direct_answer: Both `var` and `:=` declare statically typed variables. `var` works at package or function scope and can declare a type without an initial value. `:=` is shorthand for a local declaration with inferred types and works only inside functions. Use `=`—not `:=`—when every name already exists in the current scope.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand declaration, assignment, inference, and scope rather than treating the operators as interchangeable syntax.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `:=` where no name is new, or accidentally shadowing an outer variable inside a nested block.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the mixed declaration rule: an existing name may appear on the left of `:=` only when at least one non-blank name is new in the same scope.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`var` and `:=` both declare statically typed variables, but they are not interchangeable. `var` is the general declaration form and works at package scope or inside a function. `:=` is a short declaration that works only inside a function. Ordinary `=` declares nothing; it updates a variable that already exists.

`var retries int` creates an `int` with its zero value, which is `0`. This is useful when a value will be filled later or when writing the type makes the contract clearer. `name := "Ada"` needs an initializer, and Go infers `string` from that value. The variable is still statically typed after inference.

A short declaration may reuse an existing name when at least one non-blank name on the left is new in the same block. If `err` already exists, `user, err := loadUser()` declares `user` and assigns a new value to `err`. If every name already exists in that block, the statement must use `=` instead.

The new-name check uses the current lexical block. A `:=` inside an `if` or `for` block can therefore create an inner variable with the same spelling as an outer one. Use `var` for package scope, zero-value setup, or an explicit type; use `:=` for clear new locals; and use `=` when the intended variable already exists.

sections.title: One mental model: declare or update
sections.content:
First ask whether the name already exists in the current scope. If it does not, you are declaring it: use `var` anywhere or `:=` inside a function. If it already exists, use `=` to update it. The only special case is a multi-name short declaration such as `value, err := read()`: it may reuse `err` because `value` is new in the same scope.

Scope is part of the rule. A name declared inside an `if` block is different from a name with the same spelling outside that block. That is why code can compile while accidentally leaving the outer variable unchanged.

sections.title: Choose the declaration form
sections.content:
| Form | Where it works | What it does | Good fit |
|---|---|---|---|
| `var x T` | Package or function | Declares `x`; uses the zero value when no initializer is given | Package state, wider scope, or an explicit type |
| `x := value` | Function only | Declares a new local variable and infers its type | Clear local initialization |
| `x = value` | Wherever `x` is in scope | Updates an existing variable | Reassignment |
| `x, err := call()` | Function only | Declares at least one new name and may update same-scope names | Multi-result calls |

sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A{Is this inside a function?} -->|No| B[Use var]
  A -->|Yes| C{Does every name already exist in this scope?}
  C -->|Yes| D[Use =]
  C -->|No| E{Is the inferred type clear?}
  E -->|Yes| F[Use :=]
  E -->|No or explicit type helps| G[Use var]
```

sections.title: Trace the scope, not just the spelling
sections.content:
```go
package main

import "fmt"

var environment = "dev" // package scope requires var

func main() {
    var retries int          // int zero value: 0
    name := "Ada"          // new local string
    retries = 2              // update an existing variable

    value, err := load()     // both names are new here
    if err == nil {
        value, err := load() // new inner value and err: shadows both
        fmt.Println(value, err)
    }

    fmt.Println(name, retries, value, err) // outer values
}

func load() (int, error) { return 42, nil }
```

The inner statement is legal because the `if` body is a new block, but it creates new inner variables. The code after the block still sees the outer `value` and `err`.

questions.question: Where can `var` and `:=` be used in Go?
questions.title: Scope Rules for var and :=
questions.direct_answer: `var` declarations are valid at package scope and inside functions. They may specify a type, an initializer, or both, and a declaration without an initializer receives the type's zero value. The short declaration `:=` is valid only inside functions and always needs an initializer so Go can infer each new variable's type. At least one non-blank name on the left must be new in the current block. Use ordinary `=` when every name in that block is already declared; an outer variable does not count as declared in a nested block.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- `var` works at package scope and function scope; `:=` works only inside functions.
- A `var` declaration may start from a zero value; `:=` always has an initializer.
- `:=` infers types from the values on its right-hand side.
- At least one non-blank name must be new in the current block.
- Use `=` when all names already exist in that same block.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A `var` declaration is valid at package scope and inside a function. It may include an explicit type, an initializer, or both. When it has a type but no initializer, the variable starts with that type's zero value, as in `var attempts int`, where `attempts` begins as `0`.

The short declaration `:=` is a statement, so it is allowed only inside a function body. It always has values on the right, and Go infers the new variables' types from those values. `port := 8080` creates a local `int`; it does not make the variable dynamically typed.

A short declaration must introduce at least one non-blank name in the current block. After `count := 1`, `count, ok := load()` is valid there because `ok` is new, while `count := 2` is not. When every name already exists in that block, use ordinary `=`.

An outer name does not count as already declared in a nested block for the short-declaration rule. A `:=` inside an `if` can create a different inner variable and hide the outer one. When a result must remain available after the block, declare it in the owning scope and update it with `=`.

beats.recallRule: Package scope requires `var`; inside functions use `var` or `:=`, and use `=` when all names already exist in the current block.

sections.title: The current lexical block decides whether a name is new
sections.content:
A declaration introduces a name into a scope; an assignment changes the value attached to a name that already exists. `var` spells the declaration explicitly and is part of both package-level declarations and function bodies. The short form is defined as a local statement, which is why it cannot appear beside package declarations.

Type inference does not weaken Go's type system. In `port := 8080`, the untyped integer constant is given an inferred concrete type and `port` keeps that type. `var reader io.Reader = file` can be clearer when the intended interface is more important than the concrete initializer. `var buffer bytes.Buffer` also exposes a useful zero-value lifecycle without a separate constructor call.

Redeclaration with `:=` is a narrow convenience for multiple results. It is allowed only when the names were originally declared in the same block, at least one non-blank name is new, and the existing variables keep assignable values of their original types. This is common in `value, err := parse(input)` followed later by `next, err := read()`.

A nested block has its own declarations. A short declaration there may create a same-spelled inner name instead of updating the outer one. The compiler accepts both because they are different variables. When a result must survive outside the block, declare every required name before it and use `=` inside, or return the value directly so its ownership is obvious.

```mermaid
  Z -->|yes| V
  Z -->|no| C{at least one name new in this block?}
  C -->|yes| S[short declaration :=]
  C -->|no| A[assignment =]

```

sections.title: Use each form where its declaration contract is visible
sections.content:
```go
package main

import "fmt"

var serviceName = "catalog" // package scope requires var

func main() {
	var attempts int       // explicit zero-value start
	port := 8080           // new local with inferred type
	attempts = attempts + 1 // update uses =

	label, ok := lookup(port) // both names are new here
	label, found := lookup(port + 1) // label updates; found is new
	fmt.Println(serviceName, attempts, label, ok, found)
}

func lookup(port int) (string, bool) {
	return fmt.Sprintf("port-%d", port), true
}
```

questions.question: How can `:=` accidentally shadow a variable in Go?
questions.title: Variable Shadowing with :=
questions.direct_answer: Shadowing happens when `:=` declares a new variable in an inner block with the same name as an outer variable. The inner variable receives updates only until that block ends; the outer value remains unchanged. A common case is `result, err := parse(text)` inside an `if` block when `result` was declared outside but `err` is new inside. Because the current block has a new name, the statement is valid and can create an inner `result`. Declare the required variables before the block and use `=`, or return the result directly. The compiler and shadow-analysis tooling can help, but clear scope is the first defense.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- A declaration in an inner block may hide a same-named outer variable.
- `:=` checks whether names are new in the current block, not every enclosing scope.

- Narrow scopes and explicit returns make shadowing easier to notice.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Variable shadowing happens when an inner block declares a new variable with the same spelling as an outer variable. Code inside the block sees the inner variable. When the block ends, that variable disappears and later code sees the original outer value, which may never have changed.

This is easy to do with `:=` because its new-name rule is checked in the current block. If `result` exists outside an `if`, the line `result, err := strconv.Atoi(text)` inside it can declare both an inner `result` and an inner `err`. The parsed value is real, but it belongs to the inner variable.

Shadowing is not automatically wrong. `if file, err := os.Open(name); err != nil` deliberately keeps both names inside the `if` statement and its branches. It becomes a bug when later code expects an outer value to contain the result produced inside that block.

When the result is needed after the block, declare every required name in that outer scope and use `result, err = strconv.Atoi(text)`. Another clean option is to return the value directly from the branch. Both fixes make it clear which variable owns the result and prevent a successful operation from appearing to lose its value.

The parsed value is real, but it belongs to the inner variable.

Another clean option is to return the value directly from the branch. Both fixes make it clear which variable owns the result and prevent a successful operation from appearing to lose its value.
beats.recallRule: If a value must survive a block, declare it in that owning scope and update it with `=` rather than creating an inner copy with `:=`.

sections.title: A short declaration can look like an update while creating new storage
sections.content:
Go determines scopes from blocks delimited by source structure: a function body, an `if` body, a loop body, and other nested blocks can each introduce names. Name lookup uses the nearest matching declaration. Once an inner `result` exists, references inside that block resolve to it; after the block, references resolve to the untouched outer declaration again.

The multiple-assignment convenience makes the bug easy to miss. Developers often read `value, err := operation()` as “create err and update value.” That interpretation is correct only when `value` was declared earlier in the same block. If its declaration belongs to an enclosing block, the short statement can declare both names locally.

Not every shadow is harmful. An initialization clause such as `if file, err := os.Open(name); err != nil` intentionally limits both names to the condition and branches. The pattern is safe when no caller expects either name afterward. The design becomes fragile when an outer variable is part of the function's later result or state.

A reliable review traces the value beyond the closing brace. If the outer name is read later, use ordinary assignment after declaring all left-hand names in the owning scope. Guard clauses and early returns can often remove the cross-block mutation entirely. Tools that report shadowing are helpful signals, but the correct outcome still depends on whether two independent values were intended.

questions.question: When should you use var instead of := in Go?
questions.title: When to use var instead of := in Go
questions.direct_answer: Use `var` when declaring a package-level variable, when you want a variable to begin with its zero value, or when an explicit type makes the code clearer. Use `:=` for short local declarations inside a function when the initial value already makes the type obvious. Both create typed variables; the important differences are scope, initialization, and readability—not runtime speed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand where each declaration form is legal and how initialization differs.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `:=` at package scope or using it when every name on the left already exists in the same scope.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain zero values and the rule that a short declaration must introduce at least one new name.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- `var` works at package scope and inside functions.
- `:=` works only inside functions.
- `var count int` starts with the zero value `0`.
- `name := "Ada"` infers the type as `string`.
- A short declaration must introduce at least one new name.

sections.title: The idea in plain language
sections.content:
A declaration creates a variable and gives it a type. Go provides two common declaration forms because different situations need different levels of detail.

`var` is the general form. It can be used at package level or inside a function. The type may be written explicitly, inferred from a value, or left with a zero value.

`:=` is shorthand for a local declaration plus assignment. It is allowed only inside a function and requires a value on the right so Go can infer the type.

| Need | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Package-level variable | `var` | `var version = "1.0"` |
| Deliberate zero value | `var` | `var retries int` |
| Explicit interface or numeric type | `var` | `var r io.Reader = file` |
| Clear local value | `:=` | `name := "Ada"` |
| Reassign an existing variable | `=` | `name = "Grace"` |

sections.title: Choose the declaration form
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A{Where is the variable declared?}
    A -->|Package scope| B[Use var]
    A -->|Inside a function| C{Do you need a zero value or explicit type?}
    C -->|Yes| B
    C -->|No, value is available| D[Use :=]
    D --> E{Does every name already exist?}
    E -->|Yes| F[Use = for assignment]
    E -->|At least one is new| G[:= is valid]
```

sections.title: Watch the variables change
sections.content:
```go
package main

import "fmt"

var appName = "InterviewExplainer" // package scope: var is required

func main() {
    var retries int                  // int zero value: 0
    name := "Ada"                  // new local string
    retries, city := 2, "Pune"      // retries exists; city is new
    name = "Grace"                  // assignment, not declaration

    fmt.Println(appName, retries, name, city)
}
```

State after each important line:

| Line | Variable state | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `var retries int` | `retries = 0` | `int` receives its zero value |
| `name := "Ada"` | `name = "Ada"` | new local name; type inferred |
| `retries, city := 2, "Pune"` | `retries = 2`, `city = "Pune"` | valid because `city` is new |
| `name = "Grace"` | `name = "Grace"` | existing variable is reassigned with `=` |

sections.title: Two mistakes worth seeing
sections.content:
**1. Short declaration at package scope**

```go
package main
name := "Ada" // compile error: non-declaration statement outside function body
```

Use `var name = "Ada"` instead.

**2. No new variable on the left**

```go
func main() {
    count := 1
    count := 2 // compile error: no new variables on left side of :=
}
```

The second line is assignment, so write `count = 2`.

sections.title: Check your understanding
sections.content:
Predict whether each line compiles before revealing the rule:

1. `var total int` — **Yes.** It creates an `int` with value `0`.
2. `title := "Go"` inside a function — **Yes.** `title` is new and its type is inferred.
3. `title := "Go"` at package level — **No.** Short declarations are function-only.
4. `total, ok := 10, true` when `total` exists but `ok` is new — **Yes.** At least one name is new.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`var`, `:=`, and `=` do related but different jobs. `var` declares a variable and works at package scope or inside a function. `:=` declares local variables inside a function and infers their types from the values on the right. `=` declares nothing; it changes variables that already exist.

`var` is the right choice at package scope because `:=` is not legal there. It is also useful when the zero value is the intended starting state, as in `var retries int`, or when an explicit type communicates the contract, as in `var reader io.Reader = file`.

Inside a function, `:=` keeps a clear local declaration short. Later changes use `=`. A short declaration can also reuse one existing name when another name on the left is new, which is why `count, city := 2, "Pune"` is valid after `count` already exists.

A short declaration must introduce at least one non-blank name in the current block. If every name already exists there, use `=`. A nested block is a different scope, so `:=` can create an inner variable that hides the outer one. Choose among the forms by scope, zero-value intent, and readability—not runtime speed.

beats.spokenText: Inside a function, `:=` keeps a clear local declaration short. Later changes use `=`. A short declaration can also reuse one existing name when another name on the left is new, which is why `count, city := 2, "Pune"` is valid after `count` already exists.

A nested block is a different scope, so `:=` can create an inner variable that hides the outer one. Choose among the forms by scope, zero-value intent, and readability—not runtime speed.
beats.recallRule: Use `var` for package scope, zero values, or an explicit type; use `:=` for new locals; use `=` for updates.

questions.question: How do you debug a Go value that did not update after `:=`?
questions.title: Debugging a Short-Declaration Scope Bug
questions.direct_answer: When a value looks correct inside a branch but reverts afterward, inspect every `:=` between its declaration and final read. Record the file line and lexical block of each same-named variable, then check whether the short declaration introduced another name such as `err`; that can make a new inner copy. Print addresses only for addressable values if needed, or use editor references and a shadow analyzer to confirm the declarations. Fix the ownership rather than the symptom: move the declaration to the scope that needs the value and assign with `=`, or return from the branch. Add tests for both branch paths so the escaped value is verified.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Find the first line where the value differs from the expected state.
- Search backward for `:=` and mark the block containing every declaration.
- Check whether a new companion name made the inner short declaration legal.
- Use `=` only after all required names exist in the owning scope.
- Test the value after the block on both the taken and untaken paths.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
When a Go value looks correct inside a branch but returns to an older value afterward, the assignment may have reached a different variable. The useful starting evidence is the first place where the value is correct and the first later place where it is wrong. A closing brace between them makes shadowing a strong possibility.

Search between those two observations for every `:=` involving the name, then identify the lexical block that owns each declaration. Go resolves the nearest declaration, so two variables can have the same spelling. A new companion name such as `err` or `ok` often makes the inner short declaration legal.

A useful minimal example must keep the nested block and the multiple-result declaration. Removing `err` while simplifying can make the suspicious `:=` stop compiling and accidentally remove the bug. The small case should observe the value both inside and after the block.

Move every value needed later into the scope that owns the final result, then use ordinary assignment inside the branch. Returning the loaded value directly is often even clearer because no mutable value crosses the block boundary. Temporary logging can reveal the symptom, but changing the output alone does not repair ownership.

The regression test must read the value after the block, where the original failure appeared. Cover the path that enters the branch, the path that skips it, and the error path from the called function. That proves the returned or stored value—not only a nearby debug print—uses the intended declaration.

sections.title: Declaration ownership and short-assignment scope
sections.content:
Ordinary value debugging often follows assignments, but a shadow bug requires following declarations first. Write down the owning scope for the value consumed at the end of the function. Then walk backward through nested blocks and distinguish `=` from `:=`. The spelling alone cannot tell whether two references name the same variable.

A minimal reproduction should retain the block boundary and the multiple-return shape. Removing the companion `err` while simplifying can make `count := ...` fail to compile and accidentally erase the mechanism. Keep the smallest statement that still introduces one new name in the inner block, then observe the value on both sides of the closing brace.

Tooling provides complementary evidence. Definition lookup connects each use to a declaration; a debugger shows frame-local values; optional shadow analyzers flag suspicious redeclarations. Pointer addresses can demonstrate separate storage for addressable locals, but they are a diagnostic aid rather than an application fix and may distract when escape behaviour is irrelevant.

The durable repair makes one scope own the result. Predeclaration plus assignment is suitable when later statements need both value and error. A guard clause or direct return is often simpler because it avoids mutable state crossing a branch. Tests should assert the externally visible result for successful input, skipped input, and the error path.

```mermaid
  S --> D{same declaration scope?}

  D -->|yes| A[inspect ordinary assignment or callee]
  H --> O[choose owning scope]
  O --> E[predeclare plus =, or return directly]
  E --> T[test after block on every path]
```
